scenes.heading: The innate immune response
scenes.sub: Why does a cut go red, warm and swollen?
scenes.say: If a pathogen gets past your skin, say through a splinter wound, the second line of defence takes over within minutes. It explains why a cut goes red and swollen, and why you get a fever with the flu.

scenes.heading: The second line of defence
points: Non-specific: same response to any pathogen
scenes.say: The innate response is non-specific, so it reacts the same way to any pathogen. It's rapid, starting within minutes to hours. And it has no memory, so it doesn't get stronger with repeat exposure.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Emergency crews open extra lanes and race to a freeway crash
scenes.science: Inflammation brings more blood and immune cells to the injury
scenes.breaks: crews go to one specific crash, but inflammation is non-specific and has no memory of earlier 'crashes'.
scenes.say: Think of a freeway crash. Mast cells releasing histamine are the first caller to triple zero. Opening extra lanes is vasodilation: more blood, so redness and heat. Opening the barriers is leaky capillaries: swelling. Sirens guide ambulances in, like chemokines guiding cells. Neutrophils arrive first, then macrophages.

scenes.heading: Phagocytosis
steps: Membrane wraps it in a phagosome
scenes.say: Phagocytosis is like bagging rubbish for the tip. The phagocyte binds the pathogen and wraps it in a vesicle called a phagosome. A lysosome fuses with it, and digestive enzymes break the pathogen down. Waste is released by exocytosis.

scenes.heading: Other innate defenders
points: NK cells: kill cells with low MHC I
scenes.say: Natural killer cells are bouncers checking ID. Cells with missing MHC class one get killed by apoptosis. Complement proteins coat pathogens, call in phagocytes, and punch holes in them. Interferon is a smoke alarm: infected cells warn their neighbours to block viral replication.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: A cut from a rusty fence is red, warm, swollen, painful, with pus the next day. Explain.
scenes.say: Bacteria got in through broken skin. Histamine caused vasodilation, so the cut went red and warm, and leaky capillaries made it swell. Pressure on nerves caused pain. Neutrophils engulfed bacteria and died, forming pus.

scenes.heading: Fever and lymph nodes
points: Very high fever can denature enzymes
scenes.say: In a fever, pyrogens turn up the hypothalamus's thermostat. A moderate fever slows many pathogens, but a very high one can denature your own enzymes. And swollen lymph nodes mean lymphocytes are multiplying there.

Quick recap. The innate response is fast and non-specific. Histamine drives inflammation. Phagocytes engulf pathogens. And NK cells, complement and interferons back them up. Now try the practice questions!
